newsitem.title: NORWAY: Lack of water hits Hafslund profits.
newsitem.headline: Lack of water hits Hafslund profits.

text.p: Norwegian energy company Hafslund ASA on Friday attributed low water levels for hydropower production to a 14 percent drop in operating profits in the first nine months of 1996 despite a more than twofold rise in average electricity prices in the period.

One of Norway's largest power producers, Hafslund posted operating profits of 177 million Norwegian crowns ($28 million) compared with 205 million a year ago. Profit before tax amounted to 212 million crowns versus 274 million.
Earnings per share to September 30 fell 23 percent to 1.53 crowns against 1.99 crowns in the corresponding 1995 period.
"The decline in operating profit is caused by substantially lower water level in the Glomma River in the first nine months 1996 compared to last year," Hafslund said in a statement.
Electricity production declined 12 percent to 1,655 gigawatt hours (GWh) in the first nine months from a year ago.
Hafslund said water levels in the lakes Mjoesa and Oeyeren were about normal for the season.
"With normal weather conditions, the group will have a normal production situation in the fourth quarter 1996," it said.

Electricity prices in the spot market were high throughout the period due to the low snow and water level. The average price was 25.9 oere per kilowatt hour (kWh) compared with 11.8 oere per kWh in 1995.
"Even though there has been considerable rain in October and November, the prices are expected to stay high in the future as the water reservoir levels are below normal in many areas," Hafslund said.
